name: Lamentations
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text), checked against the Septuagint through Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Lamentations is untitled in Hebrew beyond its first word, ʾekah, “How!”; the Septuagint calls it Threnoi, “Laments,” and opens with a sentence not found in the Hebrew, setting the book after Israel’s captivity and naming Jeremiah as the mourner (Brenton). Hebrew tradition likewise links it with Jeremiah (compare 2 Chronicles 35:25), though the book itself names no author. The five poems lament the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. Chapters 1–4 are alphabetic acrostics: each stanza begins with the next of the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and the footnotes name each letter. Chapters 1, 2, and 4 have one verse for each letter; chapter 3 is a triple acrostic, in which all three lines of each stanza begin with the same letter (66 verses). In chapter 1 the letter ayin comes before peh, as in the standard order, but in chapters 2, 3, and 4 peh precedes ayin; some ancient alphabet inscriptions are reported to show the same peh–ayin order, and a Qumran manuscript of Lamentations (4QLam) is reported to have it in chapter 1 as well. Chapter 5 is not an acrostic, but it keeps the alphabet’s twenty-two lines, a prayer rather than a dirge. Much of chapters 1–4 is in the so-called qinah or lament meter, a long line followed by a shorter, “limping” one. English versification is used; Adonai alone is rendered “the Lord,” and the divine name YHWH “Yahweh.” This is a CJT draft; items marked for scholarly review are listed in the project review file.

verses.text:
From{h} the daughter of Zion has departed
all her splendor.
Her princes have become like stags
that find no pasture;
they went without strength
before the pursuer.

Jerusalem calls to mind,{i} in her days of misery and homelessness,
all her treasured things
that she owned in ages past.
As her people dropped into the enemy’s grip,
with no one coming to her aid,
her adversaries stared at her;
they laughed at her collapse.{j}

All{p} her people groan
as they search for bread;
they give their treasures for food
to bring back life.
“See, O Yahweh, and look,
how worthless I have become!”

I called{ab} to my lovers,
but they deceived me;
my priests and my elders
perished in the city
while they sought food for themselves
to bring back their life.

verses.text:
Their mothers{q} they keep asking,
“Where is bread, where is wine?”
while swooning like men struck down
in the town’s open places,
while their breath ebbs away
in their mothers’ laps.

What witness{r} can I offer you? What likeness find for you,
daughter Jerusalem?
What match can I set beside you, to console you,
maiden daughter Zion?
For wide as the ocean is your shattering;
who could mend you?

Your prophets’{s} visions for you
were emptiness and plaster;{t}
they did not lay bare your guilt
so as to reverse your captivity,
but the oracles they saw for you
were empty and led you astray.

They clap{u} their hands at you,
all who pass along the way;
they hiss and wag their heads
at daughter Jerusalem:
“Is this the city that was called
the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?”

“Look,{ad} Yahweh, and notice
who it is you have treated like this:
should women devour their own fruit,
infants they have nursed?
Should priest and prophet be murdered
in the Lord’s holy place?

verses.text: I{a}—a man who has looked on misery beneath the staff of his fury.{b}
Me he has driven off and made to walk in darkness and not light.
Yes, at me alone he swings his hand, over and over, the whole day long.
He{c} has worn away my flesh and my skin; he has broken my bones.
He has built siege works against me and ringed me with bitterness and hardship.{d}
In dark places he has made me dwell, like those long dead.
He has walled{e} me in, and I cannot get out; he has made my chains heavy.
Even when I cry and call for help, he shuts out my prayer.
He has walled up my ways with hewn stone; my paths he has made crooked.
A bear{f} lying in wait he is to me, a lion in hiding.
My ways he has turned aside; he has torn me to pieces; he has made me desolate.
He bent his bow and set me as a target for the arrow.
He has driven{g} into my kidneys the shafts of his quiver.{h}
I have become a laughingstock to all my people,{i} their taunt song all the day.
He has filled me with bitter herbs; he has sated me with wormwood.
He has made{j} my teeth crunch on grit; in the ashes he has pressed me down.
My soul is cast off from peace; I have forgotten what good is.
So I said, “Gone is my endurance, and my hope from Yahweh.”
Remember{k} my affliction and my wandering, the wormwood and the poison!
My soul remembers it well and is bowed down within me.{l}
Yet this I bring back to my heart; for this reason I wait in hope:
The steadfast love{m} of Yahweh never ceases;{n} his mercies do not come to an end;
they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
“Yahweh is my portion,” says my soul; “therefore I will hope in him.”
Good{o} is Yahweh to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.
Good it is that one should wait in silence for the salvation of Yahweh.
Good it is for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
Let him sit{p} alone and keep silent, when He has laid it on him;
let him put his mouth in the dust—perhaps there may be hope;{q}
let him give his cheek to the one who strikes, and be filled with reproach.
For{r} the Lord will not cast off forever;
though he causes sorrow, he shows mercy, so great is his steadfast love;
for not willingly does he humble or sadden human beings.
To crush{s} underfoot all the prisoners of the earth,
to deny a man justice before the face of the Most High,
to subvert a person in his lawsuit—does the Lord not see?{t}
Who{u} can speak a thing into being, if the Lord did not decree it?
Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that both evil and good go forth?
What grievance has a living mortal—any man—over the penalty for his sins?
Let us search{v} and examine our ways and return to Yahweh!
Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven:
“It is we who sinned and defied you; and you—you did not pardon.
You have wrapped{w} yourself in anger and pursued us; you have slain without pity;
you have wrapped yourself with a cloud, so that no prayer can pass through;
you have made us offscouring and refuse in the midst of the peoples.
They have opened{x} their mouths against us, all our enemies;{y}
panic and pitfall have come upon us, devastation and destruction;{z}
streams of water pour from my eye over the ruin of my people’s daughter.
My eye{aa} flows on and does not cease, without respite,
until Yahweh looks down and sees from heaven;
my eye torments my soul because of all the daughters of my city.
Hunted{ab} me like a bird have my enemies without cause;
they silenced my life in the pit and cast stones on me;
waters flowed over my head; I said, “I am cut off.”
I called{ac} on your name, O Yahweh, from the depths of the pit;
you heard my plea: “Do not shut your ear to my cry for help!”{ad}
You drew near on the day I called to you; you said, “Do not be afraid!”
You have pleaded,{ae} O Lord, the causes of my soul; you have redeemed my life.
You have seen, O Yahweh, the wrong done to me; judge my case!
You have seen all their vengeance, all their schemes against me.
You have heard{af} their taunts, O Yahweh, all their schemes against me,
the lips of my assailants and their muttering against me all the day.
See their sitting and their rising: I am their taunt song.
You will repay{ag} them, O Yahweh, according to the work of their hands.
Hardness of heart you will hand them; on them be your curse!{ah}
You will pursue them in anger and destroy them from under the heavens of Yahweh.”

verses.text:
How{a} the gold has grown dim,
the finest gold changed!
The holy stones lie scattered
at the head of every street.

Zion’s{b} treasured sons,
worth their weight in pure gold—
ah, now counted as clay jugs,
things a potter’s hands turn out!

The tongue{e} of the nursing infant cleaves
to the roof of its mouth for thirst;
little children beg for bread,
but no one breaks it for them.

Those who ate{f} dainties
are desolate in the streets;
those reared in scarlet
embrace dunghills.

For greater{g} was the iniquity of the daughter of my people
than the sin of Sodom,{h}
which was overthrown in a moment,
with no hands laid upon her.

Better off{l} were those slain by the sword
than those slain by hunger,
who pine away, pierced,
for lack of the fruits of the field.

The hands{m} of compassionate women
have boiled their own children;
they became their food
in the ruin of the daughter of my people.

Never{o} would earth’s kings have credited it,
nor any who live in the world,
that adversary or assailant would march
through Jerusalem’s gates.

It was{p} for the sins of her prophets,
the iniquities of her priests,
who shed in her midst
the blood of the righteous.

They staggered{q} through the streets like the blind,
soaked in so much blood
that no one dared touch
their clothing.

The breath{y} of our nostrils, the anointed of Yahweh,{z}
was caught in their pits,
he of whom we said, “Under his shadow
we shall live among the nations.”

verses.text:
Remember, Yahweh, what has happened to us;{a}
look and see how we are disgraced!

Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers,
our houses to foreigners.

Orphans we are, without a father;
our mothers are as women bereaved.

Our own water we drink for silver;
our wood comes to us for a price.

With a yoke on our necks{b} we are driven hard;
we are weary; no rest is given us.

To Egypt we have held out the hand,
and to Assyria, to get enough bread.

It was our fathers who sinned—they are gone—
yet the load of their guilt is ours to carry.

Slaves rule over us;
there is none to tear us from their hand.

At the peril of our lives we get our bread,
because of the sword in the wilderness.

Our skin is hot as an oven
from the burning heat of famine.

Women in Zion are ravished,
young women in the towns of Judah.

By their hands officials are strung up;
elders’ faces get no regard.

Young men carry the millstone,{c}
and boys stagger under loads of wood.

Gone from the gate are the old men,
gone from their songs the youths.

Our hearts’ gladness is at an end;
our dancing is changed to grief.

The crown has fallen from our head;
woe to us, for we have sinned!

Because of this our hearts are faint;
because of all this our eyes are clouded,

for Mount Zion, which lies desolate;
foxes{d} prowl over it.

Yet you, Yahweh, sit enthroned for all time;
your seat of rule stands age after age.

Why will you forget us forever,
forsake us for so many days?

Turn us back to yourself, O Yahweh, and we shall turn;
renew our days as of old—

—or have you cast us off completely,
raging against us beyond measure?{e}

notes.text: Chapter 5 is not an acrostic, but it has twenty-two verses, matching the letters of the alphabet, and its lines are mostly balanced couplets rather than the lament meter of chapters 1–4. Some Latin manuscripts are reported to title it “A Prayer of Jeremiah the Prophet.”
So a slight emendation; the Hebrew reads “Upon our necks we are pursued.”
The Septuagint reads “The chosen men lifted up the voice in weeping” (Brenton).
Or “jackals.”

The Hebrew of verse 22 (ki ʾim) is difficult; it may also be read “unless you have utterly rejected us.” In synagogue reading, verse 21 is repeated after verse 22 so that the book does not end on a note of rejection. The Septuagint reads “For you have indeed rejected us” (Brenton, modernized).
